content: The WATCh tool, developed through surveys, interviews, and collaboration with service providers and users, includes 16 outcome options. Service users identify the five most important outcomes to them, articulate their goals, and rate their current satisfaction with each outcome. A follow-up tool has been created to monitor these outcomes after wheelchair provision. The WATCh tool is currently being implemented by the NHS North Wales Posture and Mobility Service as part of routine practice, with the aim of using the resulting data to evaluate service effectiveness from the perspective of service users. Previous evaluation reports can serve as a foundation for future assessments. Evaluations, whether conducted internally or externally, are designed to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the service, enabling targeted improvements. Lessons learned are used to build on successes and inform enhancements in wheelchair provision and other relevant health or care sectors. Evaluations should lead to actionable recommendations at both service and system levels, as well as provide valuable data for national reporting on progress toward commitments such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), universal health coverage, and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Evaluation reports should ideally specify those responsible for implementing recommendations. The implementation of these recommendations requires a supportive policy environment and established financing mechanisms. National policy frameworks should ensure equitable access to wheelchairs, wheelchair cushions, postural support devices, and accessories that meet individual needs and minimum safety, performance, and reliability standards. Policies addressing wheelchair provision may include overarching policies on wheelchairs or broader policies on assistive technology provision. Cross-cutting issues impacting wheelchair provision, such as workforce guidelines and health financing policies, must be coordinated with relevant sectors. For example, workforce guidelines may influence task-sharing in service delivery, while financing policies may affect product selection. Specific examples include Colorado's Right to Repair law for power wheelchair users, which reduces repair delays by granting users and independent vendors access to parts, software, and manuals, and Norway's assistive technology system, which emphasizes repair and reuse to extend product life while maintaining quality standards. Norway's system, based on individual rights and covered by the Act on Social Security, includes multidisciplinary assistive technology centers in each province. These centers are responsible for product procurement, funding, and capacity building, with agreements made at the national level to ensure quality and price standards. Products are loaned to users free of charge and remain government property. A nationwide system collects used products, refurbishes them to high standards, and reissues them alongside new equipment. This system is particularly beneficial for children, whose needs change rapidly, as it provides well-fitted wheelchairs with minimal delays and at low cost. The repair and reuse system increases the number of people served while controlling costs. Financing wheelchair provision in line with universal health coverage principles requires planning for the costs of products and service delivery. Government funding is often the most reliable source, but partnerships between public, private, and international organizations can lead to sustainable solutions. Personal wheelchair budgets (PWBs), introduced by the NHS in England, allow users to have greater choice and control over their wheelchairs. PWBs are designed to support person-centered services and improve health and well-being outcomes. They involve thorough assessments of individual needs and goals, considering education, work, and social priorities. Funding can be combined with other sources, such as grants or charitable contributions, to increase wheelchair options. Insurance premiums and donor funding are additional sources, though they may have limitations, such as excluding marginalized groups or being short-term in nature. The next steps for the sector include mapping and strengthening relevant policies, providing guidance to manufacturers on quality standards, creating tailored service protocols for different user groups, and developing a competency framework for service roles. Dissemination of guidelines will be ensured through webinars, conferences, and workshops, targeting a broad network of stakeholders, including ministries, NGOs, professional associations, and user organizations. The WHO will use its networks to support widespread dissemination and work with partners to ensure the guidelines reach the widest possible audience. Member States are encouraged to engage diverse groups of wheelchair users in planning, implementation, and evaluation to create a supportive environment for wheelchair provision.
